articles.title: AI-Assisted Programming and Labor Demand
articles.note: Natural experiment on GitHub Copilot adoption across firms; reduced technical hiring concentrated in junior roles.
articles.abstract: Generative AI has demonstrated human-level performance on technical work tasks, yet evidence on how these task-level capabilities are changing labor demand remains scarce. We study the firm-level adoption of GitHub Copilot, an AI coding assistant, across 5,414 multinational firms accounting for 38% of the U.S. programming workforce. To identify causal effects, we exploit a natural experiment generated by firms' predetermined software procurement cycles. Early AI-adopting firms hired more workers before the launch of GitHub Copilot and had larger, more technical, and older workforces. After one year, GitHub Copilot adoption reduces quarterly technical hiring by 29% among review-induced adopters, with no effect on separations, overall technical headcount, or vacancy duration. The hiring slowdown is concentrated in the subset of junior technical roles that involve the highest share of coding work. Overall, AI coding assistance causes firms to shift demand towards more experienced workers and roles that pair some coding with broader design responsibilities.

articles.title: Boardroom Quotas and Gender Disparities in Pay and Representation: The Dutch Case
articles.note: Dutch boardroom quota effects on gender wage gap and representation across organizational levels, using linked employer-employee data.
articles.abstract: There are ongoing discussions about whether corporate boardroom quotas impact gender equality within organizations beyond the level of leadership. We examine the impact of the Dutch target law – a weakly enforced quota policy applying to a wide range of firms – on gender wage disparities and female representation across organizational levels. Our findings are ambivalent: while the quota did not reduce the gender wage gap in targeted firms relative to comparable firms, it did increase women’s representation in higher organizational wage echelons below the board. Using linked employer-employee register data and both regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences designs, we show evidence of a gradual shift towards greater gender parity in top employee income quartiles, without corresponding wage equalization. These findings highlight how boardroom quotas, even with weak enforcement, can produce compositional shifts without equalization, providing new empirical evidence and theoretical insight into the mechanisms through which institutional re-forms shape inequality.

articles.title: Rising Wages and the Decline of Low-Wage Work
articles.note: Administrative panel data on employer entry/exit versus incumbent pay changes explaining decline of low-wage work in the US.
articles.abstract: From 2014 to 2024, the share of U.S. hourly workers paid below $15 in real terms fell by two-thirds, from 38 percent to 13 percent. Why? We first distinguish the entry and exit of employers—wherein high-paying employers have supplanted low-paying ones—from organizational changes among incumbent employers. Organizational changes can be imposed on employers by external constraints, like labor market tightness, or emerge from the pursuit of new opportunities. Using panel data drawn from administrative records and job reviews, we bring this framework to bear on the recent wage gains at the bottom of the labor market. Contrary to predictions of creative destruction, we can trace only a small amount of these wage gains to the disappearance of low-wage organizations. Instead, the main driver of rising pay was low- and middle-paying incumbent employers of low-wage occupations increasing pay. These gains in low-wage occupations were associated with tightening labor markets and increased minimum wages. But over and above these external constraints, employers also pursued new opportunities for reorganizing work in low-skill jobs. Notwithstanding organizational inertia, major gains for workers’ pay can come from changes in existing workplaces.

articles.title: When GenAI Increases Inequality: Evidence from a University Debating Competition
articles.note: Randomized trial of GenAI access in university debating; high-ability participants gain more, widening performance inequality across subtasks.
articles.abstract: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) and work reports both productivity-compressing and inequality-expanding effects, leaving open a central question for organizations: Who benefits from GenAI and on which specific tasks? I address this question through a randomized controlled trial in competitive university debating, where participants are randomly assigned access to GenAI. Although most previous experimental work examines the impact of GenAI on written activities and across individuals, this setting allows me to study the impact of GenAI on a knowledge-intensive spoken activity and to identify heterogeneous effects across subtasks. I find that GenAI expands performance inequality in this setting. Consistent with recent theories on GenAI and work, results show that high-ability participants experience significantly larger gains from GenAI usage than their lower-ability counterparts in judgment-intensive subtasks, whereas lower-ability individuals only improve their performance in less expert components of debating, where GenAI can be used as a substitute. If these inequality-expanding effects generalize to similar spoken settings where complex ideas must be internalized and explained, rather than simply written, they would have important implications for understanding the impact of GenAI on work and inequality. This paper was accepted by Maria Guadalupe, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01063 .

articles.title: Generative AI And Creative Goods: Market Expansion, Crowd-Out, and Copyright
relevance_reasons: ai_work:generative ai, artificial intelligence, ai, creativ
articles.note: Difference-in-differences on a stock image marketplace policy allowing GenAI images; artist exit, output, sales, and creative work.
articles.abstract: We study how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) affects creative goods markets using data from a large stock images marketplace. In December 2022, the platform announced it would allow artists to sell GenAI-produced images, subject to two conditions: all GenAI images must be labeled, and GenAI would be prohibited in certain markets. We exploit this policy variation using a difference-in-differences design. We estimate a 136% increase in image production and 47% increase in active artists, accompanied by a 15% decline in non-GenAI production and 29% decline in non-GenAI active artists. On the demand side, total sales increase by 82%, but non-GenAI sales fall by 28% and non-GenAI sales rates decline by 3 percentage points. We use image embeddings to develop novel measures of image quality, characteristics, and market composition.We find that quality (measured as predicted sales probability) increases by 9 percentage points overall and 2 percentage points for non-GenAI content, suggesting low-quality non-GenAI artists exit. Our product characteristic measures indicate that GenAI production is heavily concentrated in characteristic space, potentially limiting the value of these images to the market. Non-GenAI production responds to GenAI by differentiating into niches. We discuss implications for copyright policy and the longer-run sustainability of original creative work.

articles.title: The Rise of Agents and the Labor Market
articles.note: Firm exposure to agentic AI linked to lower job posting growth, concentrated in non-senior jobs.
articles.abstract: We provide the first economy-wide and cross-AI model evidence on the effects of agentic AI on labor demand. We combine proprietary OpenRouter data covering about two quadrillion tokens of realized AI consumption (2 percent of global AI token consumption) across more than 400 AI models, including 1.1 quadrillion agentic tokens, with the full text of 34.8 million U.S. job postings for public firms from Lightcast. We compute our measure of firm-level exposure to aggregate agentic AI consumption (agentic beta) using the comovement of U.S. public firms' stock returns with realized weekly aggregate agentic AI token consumption. We find that a one-standard-deviation increase in a firm's exposure to agentic AI predicts 2.11 percent lower growth in job postings over the next six months and 3.20 percent over nine months. We then conduct an event study based on the release of Claude Code 2.0, which significantly expanded the capabilities of AI agents, and show that a one-standard-deviation higher pre-release exposure to agentic AI predicts 4.73 percent lower posting growth over six months post the release. Furthermore, we show that the decrease in job postings is concentrated among non-senior jobs and is statistically insignificant for senior jobs. In contrast, we find no statistically significant relation between broad AI realized consumption exposure and subsequent job posting growth once agentic exposure is controlled for. Finally, we validate our market-implied agentic exposure measure using independent evidence from firms' mentions of AI deployment in securities filings and earnings calls.

articles.title: When Does Negotiation Backfire? Gender, Job Levels, and Wage Demand Levels
articles.note: Factorial survey experiment with Japanese hiring managers on wage negotiation penalties by gender and job level.
articles.abstract: This study examines whether wage negotiation reduces hiring likelihood relative to non-negotiation, at what demand levels this penalty emerges, and how these patterns vary by the job level applied for and applicants’ gender. We argue that the legitimacy of wage demands is judged against wage standards within organizations. We conducted a factorial survey experiment with 967 individuals responsible for hiring at Japanese firms. Applicants’ gender, applied job level, and their demand levels relative to the wage standard for that level in respondents’ own organizations were varied. We then compared hiring likelihood in each condition with the non-negotiation condition using mixed-effects models. As the demand level increased, negotiation became a penalty, which emerged at lower relative demand levels for managerial than for non-managerial positions and, within each job level, at lower demand levels for women than for men. The effects of wage negotiation on hiring likelihood depend not simply on whether applicants negotiate, but on how much they demand relative to the organizational wage standard. Moreover, how much one can request without disadvantage relative to non-negotiation depends on who makes the request—a dimension of inequality distinct from inequalities in the opportunity to negotiate and in the returns to negotiation.

articles.title: AI, Specialization, and the Organization of Knowledge Work: Evidence from Legal Services
relevance_reasons: ai_work:generative ai, artificial intelligence, ai, employment
articles.note: Framework and difference-in-differences evidence on AI, self-representation, and professional-service firm pricing in US legal services.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence makes specialized knowledge cheaper to use, but its effects on professional-service firms depend on how clients reallocate work and how suppliers respond. We develop a framework linking individual self-provision, enterprise make-or-buy decisions, and pricing by specialist firms. As AI improves lower-priced alternatives, clients may reallocate work across outside providers without bringing it in-house. If the departing work is more price-sensitive than the work that remains, premium firms may raise their optimal markups even as their share of work declines. We examine these margins in U.S. legal services. Across 89 federal districts, a difference-in-differences analysis finds a 6.6-percentage-point increase in non-prisoner self-representation relative to prisoner petitions by fiscal 2025, remaining substantial after adjusting for pre-existing trends. In contrast, lawyer employment shows no clear post-2022 shift toward client firms. Legal-AI benchmarks reveal continuing limitations in reliably completing complex, multi-step work, offering one possible explanation. Meanwhile, the largest law firms reported 13% revenue growth in 2025 despite nearly flat billable hours, while lower-priced firms experienced stronger demand growth. Reported AI integration is also stronger among firms with lower revenue per lawyer. These patterns highlight the importance of changes in work allocation and supplier competition, even as much of the underlying reallocation predates generative AI. The findings illustrate why cheaper expertise need not produce either widespread internalization or declining prices for premium professional services.

articles.title: AI-Induced Social Erosion: Using LLMs for Work Tasks Reduces Help-Seeking Intentions Towards Colleagues
articles.note: Vignette experiment with 248 knowledge workers; LLM use at work reduces help-seeking intentions toward colleagues, varying by role and AI visibility.
articles.abstract: Generative AI is becoming embedded in knowledge work as an intelligent collaborator to assist in completing tasks. However, this readily available assistance risks displacing key interactions through which colleague relationships are built and sustained at work. This paper leverages the concept of help-seeking behaviour to investigate whether and how AI usage shapes colleague relationships. We conducted an online experimental vignette study where 248 knowledge workers evaluated scenarios that systematically varied whether and how AI was used across different work tasks. Using linear mixed-effects models, we found that AI-enabled work reduced help-seeking intentions compared to non-AI work across tasks, and especially for brainstorming. Visible AI usage was associated with greater help-seeking intentions towards colleagues, and individual contributors' colleague relationships were more vulnerable than managers. Our findings identify opportunities for workplace AI tools, practices, and policies to preserve colleague relationships in increasingly AI-integrated workplaces.

articles.title: Breaking Gender Norms: A Dynamic Perspective on Entering Gender-Atypical Occupations
articles.note: Longitudinal field study of newcomers in gender-atypical occupations; negative work events, task mastery, turnover intention; occupational segregation.
articles.abstract: Occupational gender segregation remains a defining feature of labor markets worldwide, and efforts to recruit individuals into gender-atypical occupations often fail because newcomers drop out shortly after entry. Understanding what drives this early attrition requires examining the day-to-day experiences of newcomers whose gender is underrepresented in their occupation, especially during the critical first weeks of organizational socialization. Integrating role congruity theory with a dynamic work-events perspective, we propose that gender-atypical newcomers experience an intensifying trajectory of perceived negative work events over time, and that this intensifying trajectory undermines their task mastery and heightens their turnover intention. Results from a longitudinal field study applying a repeated-measures design to 673 newcomers across 88 occupations over 12 weeks support these predictions. Newcomers working in gender-atypical occupations experienced a significant increase in negative work events over time, with this effect being significantly stronger for men in female-dominated occupations than for women in male-dominated occupations. Furthermore, steeper negative work event trajectories were associated with lower task mastery and higher turnover intentions. These findings advance dissimilarity research by uncovering the dynamic mechanism through which gender dissimilarity translates into adverse adjustment outcomes and contribute to the anchoring events literature by demonstrating the disproportionate and lasting influence of early negative experiences at the very outset of a professional career.

articles.title: Protective Opacity: Xenophobic Violence, Immigrant Entrepreneurs and the Erosion of Evidence on Economic Loss
articles.note: Conceptual paper on immigrant entrepreneurs reducing public profile after xenophobic violence in South Africa; documentation of losses.
articles.abstract: When immigrant-owned shops are looted, the damage is plain to everyone on the street and seldom set down in a record that an official, a court or a relief scheme could use. This conceptual paper traces part of the reason to how owners protect themselves when the state does not. Immigrant entrepreneurs who fear collective attack, and doubt that the state will protect them, may deliberately cut their business's official or public profile, a response the paper calls protective opacity. Where many owners also cut their records and independent sources cannot fill the gap, the sector would lack the records to show what it contributes and loses (a collective evidentiary externality), and losses would become harder to recognise and attribute. The paper sets out propositions on adaptation, documentation and political response, with a research design to separate the mechanism from appropriation, impunity and motivated reasoning. South Africa is used to specify the mechanism, which has not yet been tested. Its central prediction is that, where violence and political incentives are similar, localities that hold better records before an attack will document the losses that follow more completely. It also sets out disconfirmation criteria and ways to strengthen sector-level evidence without exposing individual enterprises.

articles.title: Tradeoffs between objective outcomes and human enjoyment of work in human-AI task allocation
articles.note: Behavioral experiments on how people and LLMs allocate tasks between AI and human workers, weighing enjoyment.
articles.abstract: For people, tasks at work are defined by more than their outcome: they are colored by the experience of engaging in that task. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing human-level work they may be deployed to tasks that people find enjoyable while simultaneously creating comparatively more aversive tasks such as monitoring AI outputs. This creates a thorny tradeoff for managers: whether work should be assigned purely based on the expected performance of the workers in question, or also account for the subjective experience of the person potentially doing the task. Most economic accounts focus on expected utility calculations based on the former. Here, we assess how people balance objective outcomes and more subjective qualities like enjoyment. In a series of large-scale (N=800) behavioral studies in which people allocate tasks to either an AI or human worker we find that people's allocation decisions are best captured by a model that systematically balances relative objective performance with the human worker's expected enjoyment, weighting human experience higher when a task is framed as inducing less enjoyment and adjusting based on the stakes of the task. As AI also makes decisions about work allocation, we compare a set of LLMs. We find many models also deviate from purely objective decisions, particularly when the project stakes are low, but there is wide heterogeneity as to how much and in what manner they weigh enjoyment. These results raise questions about what role human experience may play in decisions around where and how to integrate AI into workplaces. Integration may be jagged across settings due to consideration not only of the relative capabilities of workers, but also the human experience of work, the valence of that experience (e.g., more strongly weighing aversion), the context (e.g., stakes), and who is making or guiding such choices (human or LLM).

articles.title: War and Entrepreneurship: A Synthetic Control Study of the Russia-Ukraine Conflict
articles.note: Synthetic control study of firm registrations and self-employment in Russia and Ukraine during war; includes gender gap in self-employment.
articles.abstract: Is war good or bad for entrepreneurship? Entrepreneurs are often situated in extreme environments characterized by violent conflict. Yet existing entrepreneurship scholarship has largely examined war and conflict only at the micro or meso level, leaving the aggregate, macro-level entrepreneurial consequences of large-scale war underexplored. We provide a synthetic control study of entrepreneurial dynamics in the Russo-Ukrainian conflict during 2009 to 2019 as a first step toward bridging this gap. Relative to the synthetic counterfactual, registered LLCs in Ukraine declined by approximately 13% at the 2016 peak (74,000 missing firms) before recovering toward the synthetic trajectory by 2019. Self-employment in Ukraine dropped by approximately 4 percentage points (pp) at the 2015 peak, corresponding to roughly 680,000 Ukrainians no longer self-employed relative to the counterfactual, with partial recovery to a residual shortfall of approximately 280,000 by 2019. For Russia, the gap is delayed but accumulating, widening from −0.4 pp in 2015 to −1.6 pp by 2019. This corresponds to approximately 1.56 million missing LLCs relative to the counterfactual, a 32% relative loss. The contraction in Russian LLCs accumulates rather than attenuates over time. In Ukraine, we also observe a gender gap in post-2014 self-employment deviations from the synthetic counterfactual, with female self-employment falling more than male self-employment. To interpret these findings, we propose a conceptual framework that combines critical-junctures theory with the literature on entrepreneurship under authoritarian and democratic institutional regimes, arguing that the divergent post-2014 institutional trajectories of Russia and Ukraine help explain the contrasting entrepreneurial patterns we observe. JEL Codes: D74, L26, N44, O17

articles.title: Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams
articles.note: Brainstorming experiment (N=168) varying number and formation of AI partners; effects on human idea contribution, productivity, and diversity of ideas.
articles.abstract: Generative AI has improved individual productivity, but whether adding a plurality of AI partners helps or hurts remains open. We crossed AI partnership (one versus two) with behavioral formation (calibrated to average human behavior versus customized by the participant) in a brainstorming experiment ($N$=168) with human-human dyads as reference. Two-AI rooms posted more ideas to the shared board, but human-authored ideas dropped substantially. With one AI partner, formation mattered: humans paired with an average-calibrated AI posted more than any other condition. With two, this effect vanished. Humans continued talking but converted fewer ideas into board posts. AI social talk predicted more human posts, while AI posting volume predicted fewer. AI presence increased global diversity of human-authored ideas, but only a second AI increased within-session differentiation. The number of AI partners and their formation can reshape what the human contributes; single-agent results do not generalize to multi-agent teams.

articles.title: Compounding Disadvantage: Childhood Health and Black-White Economic Inequality over the Life Course
articles.note: Childhood health and Black-White earnings and employment gaps; decompositions indicate cumulative disadvantage over the life course.
articles.abstract: Childhood health has consistently been shown to predict later labor market and human capital outcomes, and many of the structural barriers that drive racial economic disparities also produce disparities in child health. Using data from the Health and Retirement Study linked to Social Security Administration earnings records, I ask whether childhood health compounds racial economic inequality across the life course. I find that poorer childhood health is associated with disproportionately large reductions in earnings and employment for Black respondents compared to White respondents. In Oaxaca-Blinder decompositions, up to 2.4% of the earnings gap and 12.2% of the employment gap can be attributed to childhood health, with contributions increasing with age in a manner consistent with cumulative disadvantage. Conversely, childhood health has little role in shaping Black wealth accumulation or Black-White wealth gaps, suggesting childhood health is a domain-specific mechanism of cumulative racial disadvantage. (Stone Center on Socio-Economic Inequality Working Paper)

articles.title: Decomposing the Gender Wealth Gap in Late Working Age: A Novel Life Course Analysis of Family and Work Characteristics in Western Germany
articles.note: Decomposition of the gender wealth gap using German panel data and life-course work and family characteristics.
articles.abstract: Women consistently hold less wealth than men, and the life course drivers of this gap remain insufficiently understood. Prior decomposition studies have focused on employment duration or cross-sectional indicators, neglecting the timing, sequencing, and complexity of both work and family life courses, and assumed common support across gender. Using German Socio-Economic Panel data, we study West Germans aged 50–59 with an innovative two-step approach addressing these shortcomings. First, life-course feature selection identifies key wealth predictors, such as education and unemployment experiences, but also family life-course characteristics and homemaking. Second, we apply the Ñopo decomposition to quantify their contribution to the gender wealth gap. Results show that family-related factors, including homemaking, and the sequencing and timing of life-course transitions decisively shape women’s lower wealth. Gender-exclusive experiences, for which there is no counterfactual, account for much of the gap, underscoring how entrenched life-course inequalities translate into lasting economic disadvantage for women.

articles.title: Dismantling organized crime's “protective umbrella”: How the downfall of corrupt officials fuels urban entrepreneurship in China
articles.note: Corrupt official downfall and organized crime protection as drivers of urban entrepreneurship in China; institutional determinants of venture creation.

articles.title: Equity crowdfunding and employee growth: the role of legitimacy and founder nationality diversity
articles.note: Equity crowdfunding, legitimacy, and founder nationality diversity in relation to employee growth of ventures.

articles.title: Gatekeepers and Kingmakers: Do Superplatforms Distort Digital Competition?
articles.note: Difference-in-differences on Google Ventures-backed startup apps on Android versus iOS; platform favoritism toward investor-backed startups.
articles.abstract: The rising dominance of superplatforms raises concerns about conflicts of interest and externalities on innovation, because they act as both marketplace gatekeepers and strategic investors. Studying Google’s dual role via Google Ventures (GV) and the Android marketplace, we find Google-backed startups receive 115% more reviews, 12% higher ratings, and 77% fewer bug complaints than their iOS counterparts—despite no major app updates. These gains are consistent with selective review removal and platform promotion. Using a difference-in-differences approach with iOS versions as controls, we isolate treatment from selection effects. Our findings challenge platform neutrality and highlight subtle mechanisms of competitive distortion. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems. Supplemental Material: The Online Appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03354 .

articles.title: Gender, Genes, and Income: How Equality of Opportunity Changed in Norway Across the 20th Century
articles.note: Twin and administrative data in Norway on heritability of lifetime income and gender equality of opportunity across cohorts.
articles.abstract: The gender income gap shrank dramatically in Western democracies over the twentieth century. We ask how genetic influences (heritability) and gendered shared environments in lifetime income changed across birth cohorts. We interpret heritability as achievement and gendered shared environments as social ascription by gender. Our data are from 11,668 twin pairs born in Norway between 1915 and 1994, linked with full-population administrative income data covering 1967–2023. The heritability of lifetime income more than tripled across birth cohorts, from 17 to 56 percent. The rise in heritability and the decline in gendered shared environments suggest growing equality of opportunity between genders over time. Yet, equality of opportunity was low until very recently, even in Norway, an extensive welfare state where gender equality has been a political priority since the 1950s. We also ask whether heritability differs between women and men, when women and men are analyzed separately. Here, heritability is lower for women, suggesting that genetic endowments are converted into income less fully for women than for men. We argue that genetically informed designs can evaluate equality of opportunity between genders, though many interpretive challenges remain.

articles.title: How effective are start-up grants for new businesses? Evidence from Romania
articles.note: Evaluates start-up grants for new businesses in Romania; entrepreneurship policy and new-venture outcomes.

articles.title: Leader Gender and Interdisciplinary Team Effectiveness: Why Trusted Collaborators Matter Most
articles.note: Archival study of 238 interdisciplinary grant teams; team composition effectiveness depends on leader gender.
articles.abstract: Despite women’s more frequent leadership roles in interdisciplinary teams, we know little about whether the same team composition structures are equally effective for female-led vs. male-led teams. We distinguish between team compositional features associated with team effectiveness generally, and whether those relationships depend on leader gender. We then examine whether the team structures most related to effectiveness are the same structures that female leaders assemble. We examined these questions using archival data from 238 interdisciplinary teams submitting grant proposals, with team effectiveness operationalized as proposal scores as evaluated by a trained committee. We examined team gender composition, past collaborations, expertise diversity, and team member status to build theory around differential effectiveness for female versus male leaders. We uncovered one central discovery, and a second, unexpected observation emerged from our central discovery. First, the relationships between certain team-composition characteristics and team effectiveness depended on leader gender. Second, the team compositional feature that was most associated with team effectiveness for female-led teams was not the feature generally observed in those teams. Our findings advance theory by showing how team composition interacts with leader gender to shape interdisciplinary team effectiveness; team composition is a leader-contingent resource whose value partly depends on leader gender.

articles.title: Temporal tradeoffs and contracting dynamics in buyer–supplier agreements
articles.note: Startup drillers' contract terms with prominent clients; moderated by serial-entrepreneur founders in oil and gas drilling.
articles.abstract: Research Summary We examine temporal tradeoffs and contracting dynamics in buyer–supplier agreements by investigating how suppliers' contractual terms change when contracting with initial clients versus new clients in the future. We use information economics and research on certifications in interorganizational relationships to delve into the mechanisms leading to potential improvements in suppliers' contractual terms. We situate the empirical analysis in the context of onshore oil and gas drilling projects to examine the liabilities for project‐related risks that startup drillers assume when contracting with client producers. Evidence indicates that when drillers initially work for prominent client producers, the drillers assume more risks in these first contracts, but fewer risks in subsequent agreements with other client producers. We argue and show that the degree to which a specific driller obtains better terms in future deals owing to its initial client's prominence will be attenuated when subsequent clients have more information on the value of the driller's resources and capabilities. Specifically, the resulting reduction in risks borne by the driller will be smaller when the driller was founded by a serial entrepreneur and when the subsequent client is vertically integrated into drilling operations. Managerial Summary This study examines the contracting dynamics that startups experience as suppliers in buyer–supplier agreements. Startups often bear more risk in initial deals to build credibility, especially when contracting with prominent clients, and such affiliations can then lead to improved terms for startups in subsequent contracts with other clients. However, this follow‐on benefit of working with a prominent client depends upon whether subsequent clients have more information on the startup's resources and capabilities. In particular, the risk‐reduction effect of working with an initial client that is prominent will be smaller for those startups founded by serial entrepreneurs. It will also be smaller when the subsequent client is vertically integrated into the value chain activities carried out by the startup. Using data from startups in the oil and gas drilling industry, we illustrate the dynamics and tradeoffs that startup drillers encounter when contracting with established client producers.

articles.title: The Consequences of Pay Standing under Pay Range Transparency
articles.note: Four studies on employee reactions to pay range transparency and pay standing; relates to pay practices within organizations.
articles.abstract: Pay range transparency—that is, disclosing the minimum and maximum pay for a job rather than individuals’ actual pay—has become the most prevalent form of pay transparency. Yet, existing theories explain employee reactions to pay information through present-focused, interpersonal comparisons with coworkers’ pay. We theorize that pay range transparency instead directs employees to interpret their structural pay standing—their pay position relative to the disclosed range boundaries—as a forward-looking signal of the organization’s recognition and structural room for pay growth. Drawing on expectancy theory, we propose that structural pay standing has a curvilinear (attenuated-positive) effect on job satisfaction, intention to stay, and job performance, mediated by pay growth uncertainty: pay near the range minimum offers weak evidence that contributions will be recognized, whereas pay near the maximum reveals limited structural room for further growth, a pattern we term a ceiling effect. Pay-related procedural justice attenuates these effects. Four studies—a natural experiment (n = 371), an online experiment (n = 603), a three-wave field study (n = 525), and an experimental-causal-chain study (n = 392)—support our theorizing, establishing structural pay standing as distinct from interpersonal pay standing and revealing an unrecognized trade-off of pay range transparency.

articles.title: Theory‐based foundations of Bayesian entrepreneurship
articles.note: Conceptual theory linking theory-based view and Bayesian entrepreneurship; explains founder-investor disagreement over opportunities and experiments.
articles.abstract: Research Summary Entrepreneurs can observe the same evidence yet reach different conclusions about an opportunity. We connect the theory‐based view with Bayesian Entrepreneurship by separating a qualitative theory of value creation—the mechanisms it admits, what it rules out, and where it applies—from the probabilistic beliefs needed to use it. The separation explains why actors disagree despite shared evidence, why different disagreements call for different experiments, and why an experiment can improve prediction without separating theories. It also distinguishes disagreement about an opportunity from differences in costs, constraints, or capabilities. When evidence is thin, a more focused theory can make acting worthwhile sooner without being more accurate. A worked theory card for Vanguard shows how to diagnose disagreement, and we outline tests of the resulting hypotheses. Managerial Summary Founders, investors, and mentors often read the same evidence differently because they hold different theories of how a venture will create value, not because one side lacks information. Before asking for “more traction,” they should state the founder's theory and its strongest rival, then locate the disagreement: whether a mechanism matters, how strong it is, which market conditions will arise, whether lessons transfer between settings, or how predictable results are. Each calls for a different test. When the parties share a forecast but differ in costs, contracts, or capabilities, the remedy is a change in terms or staging rather than another test. A worked example for Vanguard shows the method. Focused theories can justify acting sooner, but focus does not make them right.

articles.title: Why Are the Wealthiest so Wealthy? New Longitudinal Empirical Evidence and Implications for Theories of Wealth Inequality
articles.note: Norwegian administrative data decomposing top wealth into saving, inheritance, returns; entrepreneurship model explains New Money versus Old Money.
articles.abstract: We study the lifecycle dynamics of wealth inequality using 1993–2019 Norwegian administrative panel data on wealth and income. Employing a novel budget‐constraint approach, we decompose the excess wealth of the top 0.1% households relative to the median between ages 45 and 64 into higher saving rates (36%), inheritances (31%), returns (28%), and labor income (5%). One‐quarter of the wealthiest—the “New Money”—start with negative wealth on average but accumulate rapidly through high labor income and exceptionally high saving rates and returns. The “Old Money” inherit substantial wealth and grow it through above‐average though more modest saving and returns. We use these dynamic facts to evaluate five standard wealth inequality models. Although these models match cross‐sectional wealth concentration, they fail to reproduce the distinct dynamics of New and Old Money. A heterogeneous entrepreneurship model with decreasing returns to scale technology and nonhomothetic preferences is consistent with the observed dynamics.
